cases.title: Night-time hand numbness
cases.referral: 52F, R hand numbness thumb/index/middle, wakes at night and shakes the hand. NCS R arm, r/o CTS.
cases.why: Suspected carpal tunnel syndrome needs median motor and sensory studies plus ulnar studies in the same hand, so the median results can be compared with a nerve that does not pass through the carpal tunnel.

questions.q: Taken together, what pattern do your median and ulnar results show?
options: Focal median slowing at the wrist with normal ulnar studies
Diffuse slowing in both nerves, as in a polyneuropathy
Ulnar slowing across the elbow with normal median studies
Normal studies, with the abnormal values due to a cold hand
questions.explanation: The median distal motor latency and sensory peak latency are prolonged and the median SNAP is small, while the ulnar studies in the same hand are normal and the hand was warm. That is focal median slowing at the wrist, the pattern the physician will interpret in the light of the symptoms. A polyneuropathy would affect the ulnar nerve too, and the elbow segment is not involved.

questions.q: In a milder case with normal routine values, which extra study is commonly added to look for subtle median slowing at the wrist?
options: A median-ulnar comparison over the same distance (for example to digit 4)
Repetitive nerve stimulation of the abductor digiti minimi
A sural sensory study on the same side
A blink reflex study on the symptomatic side
questions.explanation: Comparison studies (median versus ulnar to digit 4, median versus radial to the thumb, or palmar mixed comparisons) measure two nerves over the same distance in the same hand, so a small median delay stands out. This app's reference lists a difference of 0.5 ms or more as abnormal. RNS, sural and blink reflex studies answer different questions.

cases.title: Little finger numbness and a weak grip
cases.referral: 61M, R numbness little finger and ulnar half of ring finger, weak grip, leans on elbows at work. NCS R arm, r/o ulnar neuropathy at the elbow.
cases.why: Suspected ulnar neuropathy needs ulnar motor studies with stimulation below and above the elbow (elbow flexed), an ulnar sensory study, and median studies to show the problem is confined to the ulnar nerve.

questions.q: Where along the ulnar nerve is the abnormality?
options: Across the elbow, with slowing and an amplitude drop above the elbow
At the wrist, with a prolonged distal motor latency
Throughout the forearm, with uniform slowing in every segment
In the median nerve, with ulnar studies within limits
questions.explanation: The wrist and below-elbow responses are normal, but the above-elbow response is smaller and the across-elbow velocity is slow compared with the forearm. That localizes the slowing and partial block to the elbow segment. The distal latency is normal and the median studies are normal.

questions.q: Why must the elbow be flexed when you stimulate and measure across it?
options: So the tape measures the true nerve length and the velocity is not falsely slow
So the nerve moves away from the stimulator and needs less current
So the hand muscles relax and the CMAP becomes larger
So the ground electrode makes better contact with the skin
questions.explanation: With the elbow straight the ulnar nerve lies slack in the groove, so the skin measurement underestimates the nerve length and the calculated across-elbow velocity looks slower than it is. Flexing the elbow (about 70 to 90 degrees) takes up the slack, so the surface distance matches the nerve. Flexion does not reduce the current needed, enlarge the CMAP or change ground contact.

cases.title: A cold hand on a winter morning
cases.referral: 28F, intermittent tingling both hands, normal exam. Arrived from outside. NCS R arm, r/o CTS.
cases.why: Median motor and sensory studies with an ulnar sensory comparison answer the CTS question. The trap in this case is temperature: measure it first.

questions.q: If you had recorded this hand without warming it, how would the results have misled the reader?
options: Prolonged latencies and slow velocities that mimic a neuropathy
Low amplitudes that mimic axonal loss in every nerve
Absent responses that mimic a complete nerve injury
Faster velocities that hide a real demyelinating neuropathy
questions.explanation: Cooling slows conduction: latencies lengthen and velocities fall, while amplitudes tend to rise. A cold hand can therefore make a healthy median nerve look like carpal tunnel syndrome or a neuropathy. It does not abolish responses or speed conduction up.

questions.q: What is the best way to deal with the low temperature?
options: Warm the limb to the lab's target and recheck the temperature before recording
Record now and apply a correction factor without measuring the temperature
Increase the current to 100 mA so that the responses are supramaximal
Lower the high filter to 500 Hz so that the slower responses look sharper
questions.explanation: Warming (warm packs, a heating lamp or warm water per lab policy) to at least the lab target, about 32 °C in the hand in this app, and rechecking is the preferred approach. Correction factors are a fallback some labs use only with a documented temperature. Raising the current or changing filters does not correct for temperature.

cases.title: Burning feet in diabetes
cases.referral: 67M, T2DM x15 yr, burning feet, reduced ankle jerks. NCS R leg, r/o polyneuropathy.
cases.why: A length-dependent polyneuropathy is screened in the longest nerves first: sural sensory, fibular and tibial motor studies in the leg. Arm studies are often added to show the gradient and exclude a superimposed entrapment.

questions.q: Which description fits these leg results best?
options: Low sensory and motor amplitudes with mildly reduced velocities
Markedly slow velocities with conduction block in every nerve
Normal sensory responses with low motor amplitudes only
Focal slowing confined to the segment across the fibular head
questions.explanation: The sural SNAP and the fibular and tibial CMAPs are small while velocities are only mildly reduced, the pattern of a length-dependent axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy. Demyelination would give marked slowing and block, normal SNAPs would point away from a neuropathy, and there is no focal change at the fibular head.

questions.q: The sural response is only a few microvolts. Which step helps you record and measure it reliably?
options: Average several sweeps and confirm the electrode placement
Set the gain to 200 µV per division so it looks cleaner
Raise the low filter to 200 Hz to remove the baseline drift
Move G1 to the medial malleolus where the nerve is larger
questions.explanation: Averaging reduces random noise while the time-locked response stays, and checking G1 behind the lateral malleolus and G2 distal along the foot rules out a placement error. A gain of 200 µV per division would make a small SNAP almost flat, a 200 Hz low filter would shrink it further, and the sural nerve runs behind the lateral, not medial, malleolus.

cases.title: Ascending weakness after a stomach bug
cases.referral: 45F, 9 days of ascending weakness and tingling after a diarrhoeal illness, areflexia. NCS, r/o GBS (AIDP).
cases.why: Suspected Guillain-Barre syndrome needs several motor nerves with proximal stimulation (to look for slowing, conduction block and dispersion) and sensory studies in the arm and leg (to look for sural sparing).

questions.q: Which features of the motor studies point toward demyelination?
options: Prolonged distal latencies, slow velocities, conduction block and dispersion
Low amplitudes with normal latencies and normal velocities
Normal motor studies with absent sensory responses only
A decrement of the response during repeated stimulation
questions.explanation: Demyelination slows conduction (long distal latencies, slow velocities), makes some fibres fail to conduct (conduction block) and spreads out arrival times (temporal dispersion). Pure low amplitudes suggest axonal loss, and a decrement on repetitive stimulation is a neuromuscular junction finding.

questions.q: The median sensory response is absent while the sural response is normal. What is this called?
options: Sural sparing, often seen in acquired demyelinating neuropathy
A length-dependent pattern of a diabetic axonal neuropathy
A technical failure of the sural recording that should be redone
A sign that the lesion is proximal to the dorsal root ganglion
questions.explanation: An abnormal arm SNAP with a normal sural SNAP is the reverse of the length-dependent pattern and is called sural sparing, a supportive finding in Guillain-Barre syndrome. A length-dependent neuropathy affects the sural nerve first. A preganglionic lesion would leave the SNAPs normal.

questions.q: Why did you need more current than usual to reach a maximal response?
options: Demyelinated nerves can have raised stimulation thresholds
The ground electrode was placed on the wrong limb
The high filter setting raises the current that is needed
Supramaximal current is lower in warm limbs than in cold ones
questions.explanation: Demyelinated or swollen nerves can need more current to excite every axon, so keep raising the current until the response stops growing before calling a response low. The ground and filter settings do not change the threshold.

cases.title: Foot drop after weight loss
cases.referral: 38M, R foot drop 3 wk after losing 15 kg, crosses legs at work, numb dorsum of foot. NCS R leg.
cases.why: Foot drop needs fibular motor studies with stimulation below and above the fibular head, plus a tibial motor and a sural study to show whether nerves outside the fibular territory are involved.

options: Across the fibular head, between the below-head and popliteal sites
At the ankle, with a prolonged distal motor latency
In the tibial nerve, with the fibular nerve within limits
In the sural nerve, with the motor studies within limits
questions.explanation: The ankle and below-fibular-head responses are normal but the popliteal response is much smaller and the across-knee velocity is slow, so the block and slowing sit at the fibular head, a common compression site with weight loss and leg crossing. The tibial and sural studies are normal.

questions.q: Which sensory study tests the sensory branch of the same nerve?
options: Superficial fibular sensory study
Sural sensory study
Saphenous sensory study
Medial plantar sensory study
questions.explanation: The superficial fibular (peroneal) nerve is a branch of the common fibular nerve and supplies the dorsum of the foot. The sural nerve comes mainly from the tibial nerve (medial sural cutaneous), often joined by a communicating branch of the common fibular nerve, so it is not a direct test of the fibular sensory fibres. The saphenous nerve is a branch of the femoral nerve, and the medial plantar nerve is a branch of the tibial nerve.

cases.title: A CMAP with a positive dip
cases.referral: 30F, healthy volunteer for a technique check. A colleague set up the median motor study; the response starts with a small positive dip.
cases.why: Only the median motor study is needed. The task is to find and fix the set-up problem.

questions.q: What was causing the initial positive deflection?
options: G1 was not over the motor point of the muscle
The stimulation was already supramaximal
The low filter was set at 10 Hz
The hand was warmer than 32 °C
questions.explanation: A CMAP should start with a sharp negative takeoff when G1 sits over the motor point. If G1 is off the motor point, the response is first seen at a distance as a positive deflection. Supramaximal current, a 10 Hz low filter and a warm hand do not cause it.

questions.q: With G1 correctly placed, an initial positive dip appears only when the median nerve is stimulated at the elbow. What is a classic cause?
options: A median-to-ulnar (Martin-Gruber) anastomosis in the forearm
Carpal tunnel syndrome slowing the distal median segment
A cold hand slowing conduction in the median nerve
A loose ground electrode on the back of the hand
questions.explanation: In a Martin-Gruber anastomosis some median-nerve fibres cross to the ulnar nerve in the forearm. Elbow stimulation then also activates ulnar-innervated hand muscles, whose volume-conducted response reaches the APB electrode as a positive dip, especially when carpal tunnel syndrome slows the median fibres. A cold hand or a loose ground does not give a positive dip at one site only.

cases.title: Neck pain and a numb thumb
cases.referral: 50M, neck pain radiating to the R thumb, numb thumb, weak elbow flexion. NCS R arm, CTS vs C6 radiculopathy.
cases.why: Thumb numbness can come from the median nerve at the wrist, the superficial radial nerve or the C6 root. Median motor and sensory and superficial radial sensory studies separate a nerve lesion from a root lesion.

questions.q: Median and superficial radial sensory responses are normal although the thumb is numb. What does that suggest?
options: A lesion proximal to the dorsal root ganglion, such as a root lesion
Carpal tunnel syndrome affecting the median nerve at the wrist
A brachial plexus lesion distal to the dorsal root ganglion
A radial nerve lesion at the spiral groove of the humerus
questions.explanation: The dorsal root ganglion lies in the intervertebral foramen, outside the dura. A root lesion is proximal to it, so the sensory axons from the ganglion to the skin stay intact and the SNAPs stay normal even though the patient feels numb. Carpal tunnel syndrome, plexus lesions and radial nerve lesions damage those axons and lower the SNAPs.

questions.q: Which test does the physician usually add to look for a radiculopathy?
options: Needle EMG including the paraspinal muscles
Repetitive nerve stimulation of the hand
A blink reflex study on the same side
A sural sensory study on the same side
questions.explanation: Needle EMG of muscles in the C6 myotome, including the paraspinals, looks for denervation in a root pattern. Repetitive stimulation tests the neuromuscular junction, the blink reflex tests the trigeminal and facial pathways, and the sural nerve is in the leg.
